# Structural Properties Inherited by Polynomial Automorphism Subgroups

This paper establishes a significant result concerning the structural properties that are preserved between a group and a particular subgroup of its automorphism group. The central question addressed is whether certain algebraic characteristics of a group are transmitted to the collection of its polynomial automorphisms, and the findings answer this question affirmatively for two important classes of groups.

## The Subgroup Under Consideration

The relevant object of study is the subgroup of the automorphism group that is generated by all polynomial automorphisms of the group in question. Rather than examining the full automorphism group, the analysis focuses specifically on this distinguished subgroup, which captures those automorphisms arising from polynomial constructions. It is precisely the structural behavior of this subgroup, in relation to the underlying group, that forms the core subject of the investigation.

## Main Results

The paper proves two closely related theorems that together demonstrate the inheritance of key group-theoretic properties.

First, it is shown that nilpotency is preserved: if the original group is nilpotent, then the subgroup of its automorphism group generated by all polynomial automorphisms is likewise nilpotent. Thus, the nilpotent character of a group is faithfully reflected in the structure of its polynomial automorphism subgroup.

Second, an analogous result is established for metabelian groups. If the original group is metabelian, then the subgroup generated by its polynomial automorphisms is also metabelian. In this way, the metabelian property, like nilpotency, is transmitted from the group to the associated subgroup of automorphisms.

## Significance of the Findings

Taken together, these results demonstrate that both nilpotency and metabelianness are inherited by the polynomial automorphism subgroup from the original group. This reveals a strong structural correspondence between a group and its polynomial automorphisms: the very properties that characterize the group's internal architecture reappear within the subgroup of automorphisms it generates. By identifying this pattern of inheritance, the paper contributes to a deeper understanding of how the algebraic structure of a group governs the structure of its automorphisms.

# Preservation of Group-Theoretic Properties Under Polynomial Automorphisms

## Introduction

A central theme in the study of groups is understanding how the algebraic structure of a group relates to the structure of its automorphism group. Given a group $G$, one may consider various distinguished subgroups of the full automorphism group $\operatorname{Aut}(G)$, each capturing different structural features of $G$. Among these, the subgroup generated by the *polynomial automorphisms* of $G$ occupies a particularly natural position, as it is intimately tied to the internal arithmetic of the group. In this work, we investigate a fundamental question: to what extent are the algebraic properties of a group inherited by the subgroup of its automorphism group generated by all polynomial automorphisms?

## The Setting

Polynomial automorphisms arise as those automorphisms that can be expressed through word-like or polynomial expressions in the elements of the group, generalizing the familiar inner automorphisms in a controlled way. When one collects all such automorphisms and considers the subgroup they generate—call it $\operatorname{Pol}(G)$—one obtains a group whose own algebraic structure may or may not reflect that of the original group $G$. It is by no means automatic that structural properties transfer from $G$ to $\operatorname{Pol}(G)$: automorphism groups are notoriously capable of exhibiting far more complicated behavior than the groups from which they are built. This makes any positive preservation result a meaningful contribution to understanding the interplay between a group and its associated automorphism structures.

We focus our attention on two of the most important and well-studied classes in group theory: **nilpotent groups** and **metabelian groups**. Nilpotent groups, characterized by the termination of their lower (or upper) central series, generalize abelian groups by permitting a bounded, hierarchical layering of non-commutativity. Metabelian groups, defined by admitting an abelian normal subgroup with abelian quotient—equivalently, by having a derived series of length at most two—form another natural generalization of abelian groups, capturing solvability of the simplest nontrivial kind. Both classes are stable under many standard constructions, yet the question of their stability under the passage to polynomial automorphism subgroups remains subtle.

## Main Results

The principal contribution of this paper is a structural preservation theorem. We prove that if a group $G$ is nilpotent, then the subgroup $\operatorname{Pol}(G)$ of polynomial automorphisms generated within $\operatorname{Aut}(G)$ is itself nilpotent. Analogously, we establish that if $G$ is metabelian, then $\operatorname{Pol}(G)$ retains the metabelian property. In each case, the defining algebraic property of the underlying group is faithfully transmitted to its associated group of polynomial automorphisms.

These results demonstrate that, at least for the nilpotent and metabelian classes, the passage from a group to its subgroup of polynomial automorphisms is a property-preserving operation. In other words, the polynomial automorphism construction respects the layered central structure of nilpotent groups and the two-step solvable structure of metabelian groups.

## Significance

Taken together, our theorems establish a genuine structural link between group properties and their automorphism structures, showing that certain fundamental features of a group are not lost but rather inherited by the natural automorphism subgroup they generate. This preservation phenomenon deepens our understanding of how automorphism-theoretic constructions interact with classical solvability and nilpotency conditions, and it suggests that similar inheritance results may hold for broader classes of groups. Beyond their intrinsic interest, these results provide useful tools for analyzing automorphism groups in situations where direct computation is intractable but the ambient group is known to be nilpotent or metabelian.

# On the Convergence of a Class of Iterative Sequences

## Abstract

In this paper, we investigate the asymptotic behavior of a family of recursively defined sequences. **We prove that** under mild boundedness conditions, every such sequence converges to a unique fixed point, and we establish explicit bounds on the rate of convergence.

## Introduction

The study of iterative processes lies at the heart of numerical analysis, dynamical systems, and optimization theory. A central question in this field concerns the conditions under which a given iteration scheme stabilizes over time.

Let $\{x_n\}$ be a sequence defined by the recursion
$$
x_{n+1} = f(x_n), \qquad n \geq 0,
$$
where $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is a continuous function and $x_0$ is a given initial value.

## Main Results

**Theorem 1.** *Let $f$ be a contraction mapping, meaning there exists a constant $0 \le k < 1$ such that*
$$
|f(x) - f(y)| \leq k\,|x - y| \quad \text{for all } x, y \in \mathbb{R}.
$$
*Then the sequence $\{x_n\}$ converges to a unique fixed point $x^*$ satisfying $f(x^*) = x^*$.*

**We prove that** the distance between successive terms shrinks geometrically. Indeed, applying the contraction property repeatedly, we obtain
$$
|x_{n+1} - x_n| \leq k^n \, |x_1 - x_0|,
$$
which shows that the sequence is Cauchy. Since $\mathbb{R}$ is complete, the sequence converges to some limit $x^*$.

Furthermore, **we prove that** this limit is a fixed point. By the continuity of $f$,
$$
x^* = \lim_{n \to \infty} x_{n+1} = \lim_{n \to \infty} f(x_n) = f(x^*).
$$

Finally, **we prove that** the fixed point is unique. Suppose $x^*$ and $y^*$ are both fixed points. Then
$$
|x^* - y^*| = |f(x^*) - f(y^*)| \leq k\,|x^* - y^*|,
$$
and since $k < 1$, this inequality forces $|x^* - y^*| = 0$, hence $x^* = y^*$.

## Conclusion

The arguments above demonstrate the power of the contraction principle. In subsequent work, we intend to extend these results to more general metric spaces and to non-expansive mappings, where the classical hypotheses fail.

---

## Setup: Polynomial maps and polynomial automorphisms

Following the framework of Passi and Leibman, one measures how far a self‑map of a group is from being a homomorphism by iterated "difference operators."

For a map $f\colon G\to G$ and $g\in G$ define
$$
(D_g f)(x) \;=\; f(x)^{-1}\,f(xg).
$$

**Definition.** A map $f\colon G\to G$ is **polynomial of degree $\le d$** if
$$
D_{g_1}D_{g_2}\cdots D_{g_{d+1}}f \;=\; 1 \qquad\text{for all } g_1,\dots,g_{d+1}\in G .
$$
An automorphism $\alpha\in\operatorname{Aut}(G)$ is a **polynomial automorphism** if the map
$x\mapsto x^{-1}\alpha(x)$ is polynomial of finite degree. Let
$$
\mathrm{PAut}(G)\;\le\;\operatorname{Aut}(G)
$$
denote the subgroup generated by all polynomial automorphisms.

The motivating example: **inner automorphisms are polynomial**, and $\gamma_g(x)=x[x,g]$ is polynomial of degree $\le c$ exactly when $G$ is nilpotent of class $c$.

## Theorem (nilpotent / metabelian correspondence)

> Let $G$ be a group and $\mathrm{PAut}(G)$ the subgroup of $\operatorname{Aut}(G)$ generated by its polynomial automorphisms.
>
> **(1) Nilpotent case.** $G$ is nilpotent of class $\le c$ **iff** every inner automorphism of $G$ is polynomial of degree $\le c$; in this case $\mathrm{PAut}(G)$ acts *unipotently* on $G$ (relative to the lower central series), and $\mathrm{PAut}(G)$ is itself nilpotent, with class bounded by a function of $c$.
>
> **(2) Metabelian case.** $G$ is metabelian (i.e. $G''=1$) **iff** the polynomial automorphisms generate a **metabelian** group $\mathrm{PAut}(G)$; equivalently, the commutator of any two polynomial automorphisms again acts as a polynomial map into the abelian subgroup $G'$, so that $\mathrm{PAut}(G)''=1$.

## Remarks

- Part (1) is the group‑theoretic reflection of the classical fact that nilpotency of class $c$ is equivalent to the inner automorphism action being unipotent of length $c$; polynomiality of degree $\le c$ is exactly this unipotence expressed through the difference operators $D_g$.

- Part (2) uses that in a metabelian group the derived subgroup $G'$ is abelian and is a $\mathbb{Z}[G/G']$‑module; the polynomial automorphisms then act through this module structure, forcing the group they generate to be (abelian)-by-(abelian).

- The bracketing of the two statements exhibits the general principle: **structural conditions on $G$ (nilpotency, solvability of small derived length) are detected by, and mirrored in, the subgroup of $\operatorname{Aut}(G)$ generated by polynomial automorphisms.**
